pr_body:
Provides "true" cancellation for async ping methods using either a token or
the existing SendAsyncCancel() API.

Fix #67260
pr_comments:
Note regarding the `new-api-needs-documentation` label:

This serves as a reminder for when your PR is modifying a ref *.cs file and adding/modifying public APIs, to please make sure the API implementation in the src *.cs file is documented with triple slash comments, so the PR reviewers can sign off that change.

Issue Details
Provides "true" cancellation for async ping methods using either a token or the existing SendAsyncCancel() API. Fix #67260
Author: madelson
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Net`, `new-api-needs-documentation`
Milestone: -

> One callout is that this does not implement true cancellation on Windows because Windows pings [use a native function](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Net.Ping/src/System/Net/NetworkInformation/Ping.Windows.cs#L170) which wasn't obviously cancelable from my read of the docs (let me know if I missed something). Maybe this is something that can be handled by [CancelIOEx](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/cancelioex-func)?

It would be nice to have consistent behavior between platforms if it can be achieved, I did a quick test and CancelIO didn't work (returned INVALID_HANDLE). Not sure if using raw ICMP sockets is viable, maybe @antonfirsov will know.

> One callout is that this does not implement true cancellation on Windows because Windows pings [use a native function](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Net.Ping/src/System/Net/NetworkInformation/Ping.Windows.cs#L170) which wasn't obviously cancelable from my read of the docs

I've not read the change yet. What do you do in this case? If it's just not as cancelable, e.g. once the native call is made the cancellation token is ignored, that's ok. If instead cancellation triggers the returned task to complete even while the native operation continues, that's not ok.

> One other option I considered was changing the Windows ping to use raw sockets when possible (as is [done for Unix](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Net.Ping/src/System/Net/NetworkInformation/Ping.Unix.cs#L32)). However, I'm not sure of the pros/cons there.

IIRC, creating raw sockets requires elevated/admin privileges. If that's the case, we can't do that.

@stephentoub 

> I've not read the change yet. What do you do in this case? If it's just not as cancelable, e.g. once the native call is made the cancellation token is ignored, that's ok. If instead cancellation triggers the returned task to complete even while the native operation continues, that's not ok.

It is much closer to the former than the latter but not exactly. Before this change, we already had a (mostly non-functional) version of cancellation via the `Ping.SendAsyncCancel()` method which would just set the `_canceled` flag. When the async operation completed, [we'd convert to a canceled result based on the task](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Net.Ping/src/System/Net/NetworkInformation/Ping.Windows.cs#L290). **I didn't change this code at all for the Windows branch.** The only change in the behavior is that previously cancellations were getting wrapped as `PingException` and now cancellations flow through without wrapping so that all cancellations manifest in the same way.

> IIRC, creating raw sockets requires elevated/admin privileges. If that's the case, we can't do that.

In Unix, we [use the raw socket version conditionally based on whether we have permissions](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Net.Ping/src/System/Net/NetworkInformation/Ping.Unix.cs#L32). I was proposing that we do the same thing for Windows. Maybe you're just saying that people running in admin mode is so rare that having this fork isn't worth it? Or maybe you're saying that the permission check for Unix doesn't work on Windows?

Thanks for all the feedback @rzikm @stephentoub . At this point I'm just waiting on resolutions to a few open threads:

* https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72338#discussion_r922843165
* https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72338#discussion_r946258155
* https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72338#discussion_r946262570
Looks like there is just one thing to address https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72338#discussion_r946258155 and we will be good to go, right? @madelson?

Issue Details
### Background and motivation This was already approved in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/14336, but reverted in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/67253 because this requires some more work. See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/64860#discussion_r836496120 ### API Proposal ```cs namespace System.Net.NetworkInformation { public class Ping { public Task SendPingAsync(IPAddress address, TimeSpan timeout, byte[]? buffer, PingOptions? options, CancellationToken cancellationToken); public Task SendPingAsync(string hostNameOrAddress, TimeSpan timeout, byte[]? buffer, PingOptions? options, CancellationToken cancellationToken); } } ``` ### API Usage - ### Alternative Designs _No response_ ### Risks _No response_
Author: deeprobin
Assignees: -
Labels: `api-suggestion`, `area-System.Net`, `untriaged`
Milestone: -
Updated to match what was approved.
@danmoseley Thanks. I removed the trailing `+`. Can you remove the `untriaged` label?
Ping will almost always wait, so I think `Task<>` is fine. No need to optimize the no wait case
IMO, this proposal can be combined with #34856
@sakno Could be. But this is already approved and #34856 is not.

I have some interest in working on this.

One thought: could `TimeSpan timeout` be changed to `TimeSpan? timeout = null`? This would allow you to fall back to the default timeout as is possible with the `int` timeout APIs.

review_comments: Doing this here means the timeout won't apply to the GetHostAddressesAsync inside getAddress.  Why is that ok / desirable?  I'm also unclear as to why this is being done like this after the SendPingAsyncCore.  Normally this kind of ordering would be to avoid a race condition, but that doesn't apply here.

Both of these are attempts to maintain the existing behavior / be true to the documentation:

* The old code does not apply the timeout to `Dns.GetHostAddressesAsync` (see https://source.dot.net/#System.Net.Ping/System/Net/NetworkInformation/Ping.cs,646).
* The documentation for [the `timeout` parameter](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.networkinformation.ping.sendpingasync?view=net-6.0#system-net-networkinformation-ping-sendpingasync(system-string-system-int32-system-byte()-system-net-networkinformation-pingoptions)) says: "The maximum number of milliseconds (*after sending the echo message*) to wait for the ICMP echo reply message". 

I feel like the timeout is supposed to be inherent to the ping request, rather than being a general timeout for the entire operation. In contrast, I think the `CancellationToken` is the way for the caller to abort the operation whenever they want. Thoughts?

I'll defer to @dotnet/ncl on the desired behavior here.  I expect it was documented that way because there was literally no way before for the Dns operations to be timed out.  But there is now.  The question then is whether we want to update the timeout to apply to the whole operation or just to the waiting for the ICMP echo reply message; I'm ok either way.

I've not looked; are we consistent with the timeout only applying to the ICMP echo reply across all implementations?

Personally, I feel like it is better to keep the timeout only for the ICMP echo reply. As noted, users can use the `CancellationToken` to cancel the operation *x* ms from the start of it, and if we make the `timeout` parameter cover the DNS resolution as well, users may get different results depending on whether DNS was fast enough or was/wasn't cached.

As mentioned [here](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/67260#issuecomment-1185972901), I think this API would be more useful if `timeout` were an optional parameter. Requiring it here when other overloads allow you to skip it will likely lead to either poorly-chosen timeouts or copying the default value.
@rzikm thoughts on this change?
I would stick to what was approved during the API review, any changes to that need to be green-lighted by the API review group.
_Many_ APIs throughout the core libraries accept a timeout, none to my knowledge accept a nullable TimeSpan, and we wouldn't diverge for this one method.

> as a caller I wouldn't know what a "reasonable" default timeout was

A user has a much better chance of picking an appropriate timeout for their use case than we do.

Makes sense thanks @stephentoub , especially if this would be a new pattern. I'll note that other existing Ping overloads *do* use a default timeout (5s), but it sounds like we're moving away from that rather than trying to match it.
I figured it didn't hurt to also allow timing out / canceling while reading the output, but  calling it out in case it isn't desirable.

I'm surprised that this doesn't need to be `volatile` since it gets written to and read from on different threads, with the reads eschewing a lock (but I'm not an expert on such things). With the updated code the read pattern is unchanged (no lock), we now write to this outside of a lock sometimes (from the cancellation token registration); does that change anything?

Since this is always set together with cancelling the _`timeoutOrCancellationSource`, I think we can get away without volatile, but I will defer to the opinion of the more experienced. cc: @stephentoub

It doesn't. There's always a happens-before relationship involved, e.g. the flag is set before the asynchronous operation is started, or it's read only after the things that could have set it have demonstrably quiesced.
Dispose doesn't Cancel.  Do you want to also Cancel?  I'm just wondering about the comment on this method which suggests it does so.

Interesting. I feel like this comment is just wrong. The way the method used to and still works is that if called while a ping request is in progress it sets `_disposeRequested` to true and then returns. Then when the ping request completes it calls `Finish` which completes the disposal.

It would be interesting if this comment implied that what `InternalDisposeCore` does (disposing the handles) can actually safely cancel outstanding Windows ping requests, but given that the [old .NET Framework version](https://referencesource.microsoft.com/#System/net/System/Net/NetworkInformation/ping.cs,131) seems to have the same behavior I'm not convinced. 

Do you agree? Should I just remove the comment? Should we change the code to start canceling the token once we've requested disposal to hurry outstanding requests along?

> I feel like this comment is just wrong.

Looks like you're right. You can just delete it.
You should be able to mark this method as `[MemberNotNull(nameof(_timeoutOrCancellationSource))]`, which should let you remove at least one if not more `!`s on use of that field.
Do you mean other methods? This is the one that lazily initializes the `CancellationTokenSource` (`Finish` then nulls it out if it has become canceled).
I mean putting that attribute on this method should let you remove the `!` from other methods that call this one.
I did this to reduce logic duplication between the `IPAddress` and `string` paths, but let me know if I should unwind it to keep things how they were before.

Previously, cancellations using `SendAsyncCancel()` would get wrapped in `PingException` in the try-catch below. That didn't seem very desirable to me, so I changed it to return a canceled task regardless of how cancellation occurred. Curious what others think.

Other options would be to always wrap, or preserve the wrapping behavior for `SendAsyncCancel()` only.

That would probably be a breaking change in the behavior, but since we are implementing "true" cancellation and change the behavior, it might be okay (and we just need to make sure it is documented).

Tagging @stephentoub for more thoughts.

> we just need to make sure it is documented

@rzikm Do you mean in the doc comments of the new APIs?

> since we are implementing "true" cancellation and change the behavior, it might be okay

FWIW as a consumer of .NET async APIs, it is frustrating when cancellations get wrapped to look like some other type of exception.

> Do you mean in the doc comments of the new APIs?

I meant in release notes that are compiled and list breaking changes. It would be handled by us. AFAIK, we don't list `TaskCancelledException` in docs for async methods.
